title: Learning before breakfast
hook: the day begins with a blessing over Torah, then a little study straight away

segments.voice: Yesterday, peah and the deeds without measure. Your line was no limit on kindness. Today, the blessing that comes just before that list.

A lot of mornings start by taking something in. Headlines. Messages. Somebody else's photos of somebody else's breakfast. Whatever comes first tends to set the weather for the morning. The Jewish prayer book has an opinion about what should come first. Very early, before the psalms, before the main prayers, before a single request, there's a blessing for studying Torah. Then, so the blessing isn't left hanging, a few lines to actually study, on the spot.
screen: `WHATEVER COMES FIRST SETS THE WEATHER.` → `A BLESSING FOR STUDY.` → `THEN STUDY, ON THE SPOT.`

segments.voice: The blessing comes from the Talmud, tractate Berakhot, where several rabbis each offer a wording, and the prayer book keeps more than one. The first thanks God who commanded us la'asok b'divrei Torah, to busy ourselves with the words of Torah. Not just to read, or to finish, but to be busy with it, the way you're busy with work. The next asks: make the words of Torah sweet in our mouths, and in the mouths of our children and their children. Sweet, the way honey is sweet. And the last is the one the Talmud calls the finest of blessings: who chose us and gave us the Torah. Then come a few lines of study, so the blessing has something to bless. In many prayer books, first the priestly blessing from the Book of Numbers, in the old Jewish translation: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee." Then the lists from yesterday, from the Mishnah and the Talmud. A verse of Torah, a mishnah, a passage of Talmud: a taste of each layer of the tradition. The Talmud takes this blessing seriously. In tractate Nedarim, it even suggests that when learned people's children didn't become learned, it was because their parents hadn't blessed the Torah first. Study, in this telling, isn't only information. It's a gift, received with thanks before you open it.
screen: `TO BUSY OURSELVES WITH TORAH.` · `MAKE THE WORDS SWEET.` · `THEN A FEW LINES, RIGHT AWAY.` · `RECEIVED AS A GIFT, WITH THANKS.` · then, large: `LEARN SOMETHING FIRST.`

segments.voice: Pick up something worth learning from: a page of scripture, a book you trust, even a line from today's lesson. If you pray, first say la'asok b'divrei Torah, to busy ourselves with the words of Torah; if not, take one breath of thanks for being able to read. Then read one line, slowly, twice.
Divrei Torah. Words of Torah — the morning blessing asks to be busy with them, then the prayer book gives a few lines to study on the spot.
Your line: learn something first. In the prayer book, study comes before a single request. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 548 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BINDING IN THE MORNING.`

howItsDone: Jews who pray each morning say the blessings over the Torah early in the service, then immediately read a few short passages, often the priestly blessing, a mishnah and a passage of Talmud, so the blessing covers the day's study.

Because the prayers don't count until you've finished a full page of Talmud.
It's a warm-up for the rabbi's sermon, the main part of the morning.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'a verse, a law, a story' was inaccurate for the study passages; now 'a verse of Torah, a mishnah, a passage of Talmud'. The practice no longer confuses the priestly blessing with the Torah blessing. Softened 'most of us'; the carry now starts today.

Berakhot 11b: the several wordings (la'asok b'divrei Torah; veha'arev na; asher bachar banu, called 'the finest of blessings' by Rav Hamnuna); confirm attributions and the claim that the siddur combines them (Ashkenazi practice; some rites differ on la'asok vs al divrei Torah).
Study passages after the blessings: priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24–26), Mishnah Peah 1:1, Shabbat 127a in many Ashkenazi siddurim; Sephardi rites differ. Confirm.
Nedarim 81a: why scholars' children are not scholars, 'because they did not bless the Torah first'; confirm.
